newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New cabinet, summit make decisive week for Russia.
newsitem.headline: New cabinet, summit make decisive week for Russia.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin is set to unveil a long-awaited cabinet reshuffle this week before holding key post-Cold War summit talks in Finland with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
In a decisive week for Russia, the results of arduous behind-the-scenes bargaining at home and abroad should finally come out into the open.

Horse-trading over a new government line-up to tackle the ailing economy has dragged on for more than two weeks, accompanied by furious media speculation over who might join the cabinet and whether they would make any difference.
U.S. and Russian officials, meanwhile, have been trying to hammer out a deal that Yeltsin and Clinton can announce at their summit in Helsinki to ease tensions over NATO's expansion plans.

"The toughest negotiations are underway on the structure and personel of Russia's cabinet in the entire period since the collapse of the Soviet Union," leading television anchorman Yevgeny Kiselyov said on Sunday.

The Kremlin said on Friday that Yeltsin would reveal the cabinet line-up before leaving for the Helsinki summit, expected to be dominated by the highly-sensitive issue of NATO's plans to invite some of Moscow's former allies to join the alliance.

Yeltsin has laid out stiff terms for any softening of Moscow's objections to NATO's plans, saying he would insist on a legally-binding treaty barring Western forces from ever being stationed in eastern Europe.
Moscow's ambassador to Prague warned the Czech Republic, likely to be one of the first in line to join NATO, that it risked upsetting key bilateral agreements with Russia if it did so.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov held talks in Washington over the weekend to try to forge a breakthrough before the summit, but U.S. officials remain publically opposed to a legally binding treaty and other Russian demands.
The start of the two-day summit has been postponed for a day, until Thursday, to allow Clinton to recover from knee surgery after a fall last week.

Kiselyov, who presents NTV commercial television's influental Itogi current affairs programme, quoted government sources as saying Yeltsin would put the final touches to the new cabinet at a meeting in the Kremlin on Monday.

Leading opposition communist Gennady Seleznyov said the delay indicated fierce disagreements between Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, a relatively conservative industrialist, and reformer Anatoly Chubais, who has been made his deputy.

"If the unlucky people who worked on privatisation with Chubais will take high office nothing good will happen," said Seleznyov, referring to popular discontent with the mass privatisation programme which followed communism's collapse.

Many Russian distrust Chubais, believing that the reforms he led when he was last in the government unleased a huge wave of corruption and allowed a privileged few to get rich at the expense of the majority.

But Kiselyov said that a move last week to end some tax breaks enjoyed by several big companies meant that Chubais, appointed by Yeltsin 10 days ago to try to solve huge tax and and wage arrears, was serious about cleaning up reform.

"Chubais...and other members of the team are clearly prepared to put the interests of reform in Russia's economy above any corporate interests," he said. "In the eyes of the banking and industrial corporations they now look virtually like traitors."
